newsitem.title: UK: Studies find more genetic links to diabetes.
newsitem.headline: Studies find more genetic links to diabetes.

text.p: Researchers said on Thursday they had found more evidence of the complex genetic causes behind diabetes and said their findings could help find better treatment for the disease.
Two separate reports in the science journal Nature described genes directly linked to type-II diabetes, which affects two percent of the world's population.
In this case the variation of type-II diabetes involved is maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), caused when a person inherits one copy of a defective gene.

Graeme Bell and colleagues at the University of Chicago found a mutation in a gene known as hepatocyte nuclear factor-1 alpha (HNF-1a), a gene that had been known to have involvement in liver function, also led to diabetes.
A second report found a mutation in another gene, HNF-4a, was also involved.

"It is clear from our work that there are many genes acting together to cause late-onset diabetes," said Roger Cox, a molecular biologist at Oxford Univeristy, who helped work on the second study. "These are two genes in a multi-gene family."
Cox said the findings would help doctors target better treatments for diabetes, which can endanger pregnant women or can lead to blindness, gangrene and kidney failure.
"It does point to a list of genes that we can now go on to test," he said. "It opens up a new area of research."
Diabetes occurs when calls in the pancreas known as islet cells fail to produce insulin properly. Insulin helps regulate blood sugar levels.

Bell's group said it was not clear how inheritance of just one bad gene could cause a person to have diabetes. "It is possible that a partial deficiency of HNF-1a could lead to beta cell (the islet cells in the pancreas) dysfunction and diabetes," they wrote.
John Todd of Oxford University's Wellcome Trust Centre for Human Genetics said the findings were important news.

But he noted that the genetic background to diabetes was turning out to be complex and many more genes remained to be found. "Which genes modify the severity of MODY; for example, mutations that increase the sensitivity of tissues to insulin?" he asked.
